judge_assessment.explanation: Every value the judge quotes checks out. The books plot draws stacks of 4, 6, 3, 2, 1 above 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — so 16 children in all, the tallest stack is above 3 and holds six X's, and the shortest is above 6 with one. The shell list 5, 7, 6, 8, 6, 5, 7, 6, 10, 7, 6, 8 gives 5:2, 6:4, 7:3, 8:2, 9:0, 10:1, which is 12 shells, five distinct lengths, and a range of 10 - 5 = 5; the partial plot in problem 6 pre-draws exactly the 5's, 7's and 8's, so the child draws four X's above 6 and one above 10, matching the judge's 'shell frequencies 4 and 1'. Item 10(b) is correctly typed manual with a strong rubric. Two things the judge did not test. First, coverage: eight of the ten problems print more answer blanks than verify.json covers. Problem 2 prints the tallest-stack label AND 'How many X's are in that stack?' against one max_key entry, so the value 6 is unchecked; problem 3 prints five per-stack blanks plus the total against one total entry; problem 4 prints 'How many children was that?' (1) unchecked beside its min_key entry; problems 5 and 8 each print the two stack sizes before the difference; problem 6's 'Above 10?' (1) has no entry; problem 7's 'Does your answer match how many lengths were on her list?' has none; problem 9 prints 'Longest shell: ____' and 'Shortest shell: ____' (10 and 5) beside its range entry. Second, problem 6 asks the child to DRAW the missing X's onto a partially built plot — the sheet's one construction task, and the reason the contract's build-a-line-plot facet exists — and it is recorded as an ordinary read_data check on the resulting frequency, with no manual companion. The drawn plot itself is never declared as something a human must look at, and final_response.md reports only problem 10 as flagged.

strengths_to_preserve: The three-stage structure is a genuinely good fluency ramp and is worth keeping verbatim: read a finished plot (1-5), BUILD one from a raw measurement list (6), then read the finished version of the plot you just built (7-10) so the child self-checks their construction before answering questions that depend on it. Problem 7's stem even says so: 'Here is the finished plot. Check yours against it before you go on.'

Problem 8's trap is the exact confusion the topic turns on — 'subtracted the two lengths written under the line instead of the numbers of X's above them', declared with value 1 against the correct 2 — and the key names the two kinds of number on a line plot as the sheet's organising idea.

Problem 9 keeps the units straight where the rest of the sheet is unitless: the range answer declares answer_unit 'cm', the sheet prints 'Answer: ____ cm', and the key explains that this answer is a length while the neighbouring answers are counts.

Item 10's manual desc states what an answer must contain AND what to reject ('Do not accept an answer that only says Sam is wrong without saying what the empty space above 9 tells you'), which turns an open item into something two graders would mark the same way.

The zero-frequency value at 9 cm is deliberate and load-bearing: the data set was chosen so one labelled position carries no X's, which is what makes problem 10's misconception (rub the 9 off the line) available at all.

root_causes.description: No gate compares printed answer blanks against covered verify entries, so a sheet built on scaffolded sub-readings records one check per problem while the child writes three to six numbers. Every unchecked value here is determinate and derivable from the same data dict that draws the plot, which is what makes the omission fixable and also what makes it invisible today.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 3 prints 'Above 2: ____ Above 3: ____ Above 4: ____ Above 5: ____ Above 6: ____' and 'Children in Room 4 altogether: ____' — six blanks; verify.json id 3 is one read_data total entry, expected 16.

worksheet.pdf problem 2 prints 'Which number of books has the tallest stack? ____' and 'How many X's are in that stack? ____'; verify.json id 2 is one max_key entry, expected '3' — the stack height 6 is unchecked, and the key itself flags the two answers as different numbers ('Both questions point at the same tall column, and the two answers are different numbers (3 and 6)').
worksheet.pdf problem 9 prints 'Longest shell: ____', 'Shortest shell: ____' and 'Answer: ____ cm'; verify.json id 9 is one stats range entry, expected 5.
worksheet.pdf problem 6 prints 'How many X's did you draw above 6? ____' and 'Above 10? ____'; verify.json id 6 covers only the value at 6 (expected 4).
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints one value per problem (1. 3, 2. 3, 3. 16, 4. 6, 5. 3, 6. 4, 7. 12, 8. 2, 9. 5, 10. 0).

root_causes.description: The sheet's one construction task — drawing the missing X's onto a partially built line plot — is recorded as a read_data check on a frequency the student is asked to report, so the constructed artifact itself is neither verified nor declared for human review. SKILL.md line 257 explicitly lists 'graph sketches' among the things 'manual' exists for.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 6: 'The X's for the 5's, the 7's and the 8's are already drawn. Cross each of those off the list, then draw the X's that are still missing.'

verify.json id 6 is a single {"type": "read_data", "query": "value", "key": "6", "expected": 4} entry, and its facet is 'build-a-line-plot' — the entry is tagged as the construction facet while checking only a reported number.
verify.json's only manual entry is under id 10; machine_observation reports gate_chain_manual_flags: true on the strength of that single item.
SKILL.md line 257: 'Use manual for: graph sketches, sign charts, word problem setups ... and any explanation/reasoning answer.'

improvements.title: Count printed answer blanks per problem and require one covered verify entry for each
improvements.proposed_change: In tests/check_answer_line.py (already receives the worksheet .tex and verify.json; already gate 10 in build.sh), count \ansblank / \ansline / \answerline per segmented problem region, add the one line the \problem macro emits when its workspace argument is positive, and compare with the number of verify entries for that id carrying an 'expected' value or "type": "manual". Exit 1 on an undercount with both counts and the problem number. For curr-097 the fix is additive JSON against data already present: id 2 gains the tallest-stack height (6), id 3 the five per-stack values, id 4 the shortest-stack count (1), ids 5 and 8 the two stack sizes each, id 6 the 'above 10' value (1), id 9 the max and min (10 and 5). Problem 7's 'Does your answer match?' is a yes/no self-check rather than a graded answer and should either be recorded or moved out of an answer blank into the stem.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/slot_undercount_lineplot/ with a worksheet problem printing 'Which number has the tallest stack?~\ansblank How many X's are in that stack?~\ansblank' against a verify.json id-1 entry of {"type": "read_data", "query": "max_key", "expected": "3"}. Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 reporting '2 printed answer slots, 1 covered'; add {"type": "read_data", "query": "value", "key": "3", "expected": 6} and assert exit 0.
improvements.expected_impact: On this sheet, coverage rises from 11 checked values to roughly 25, and the Quick Answers bank becomes usable for marking — today a grader reading '3. 16' has six blanks to mark from one number. Across the run it closes the largest verification gap (61 cases).
improvements.risk: The scaffolded sub-readings are good design and a heavy-handed gate could drive authors to remove them. Lead the failure message with 'declare the value', and state in SKILL.md that scaffolds are encouraged provided their answers are recorded. Getting the \problem auto-emitted line counted exactly once is the implementation hazard.

improvements.title: A construction task (drawing onto a plot) needs a manual entry, not just a check on the number it produces
improvements.proposed_change: Add the open-response stem scan to tests/check_answer_line.py covering construction and marking verbs ('draw', 'sketch', 'plot', 'complete the', 'circle', 'mark', 'shade') as well as explanation verbs, and exit 1 when the matching id has no {"type": "manual"} entry. For curr-097, id 6 keeps its frequency checks and gains a manual entry describing what the finished plot must look like — 'four X's above 6 and one above 10, added to the pre-drawn 5's, 7's and 8's; the completed plot must show 5:2, 6:4, 7:3, 8:2, 9:0, 10:1' — which is information the answer key already carries as a printed finished plot in problem 7. Reinforce it in SKILL.md next to the existing 'Use manual for: graph sketches' line, which already states the rule the sheet did not follow.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/construction_unflagged/ with a worksheet problem reading 'The X's for the 5's, the 7's and the 8's are already drawn. Draw the X's that are still missing. How many X's did you draw above 6?~\ansblank' against a verify.json id-1 holding only the read_data value entry. Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 naming problem 1 and the verb 'draw'; append a manual entry and assert exit 0.
improvements.expected_impact: The one item on the sheet where a child produces a drawing stops being reported as fully machine-verified. The grader is told to look at the plot, not only at the two numbers the child copied off it — which matters because a child can report '4' and '1' correctly while stacking the X's in the wrong columns.
improvements.risk: 'draw' and 'plot' appear in incidental prose, so scan stem text only with comments blanked. There is also a judgement call the gate cannot make — a construction whose result is fully pinned by later items (as here, since problem 7 prints the finished plot) is less at risk than a free sketch — but declaring it manual costs nothing and the exit-2 path already exists.

case_summary: The mathematics and the figures are right: I re-counted every stack on both plots and re-derived the shell frequencies from the printed list (5:2, 6:4, 7:3, 8:2, 9:0, 10:1), confirming 16 books, six children at 3 books, 12 shells and a range of 5, with the deliberate empty position at 9 cm that makes the closing misconception item possible. The read-build-reread structure is a genuinely strong fluency ramp and item 10(b) is declared manual with a rubric that tells a grader what to reject as well as what to accept. Two contract defects sit underneath. Eight of the ten problems print more answer blanks than verify.json covers — problem 3 prints six blanks against one total, problem 9 asks for the longest and shortest shell beside its range entry, problem 2's stack height of 6 is unchecked even though the key calls out that 3 and 6 are different answers to adjacent questions — so a grader working from the Quick Answers bank has one number per problem for a sheet that asks the child to write three to six. And problem 6, the sheet's one construction task, is recorded as a read_data check on a reported frequency with no manual companion, though SKILL.md lists 'graph sketches' as the archetype for the manual type. Every missing value is already derivable from the data dicts that draw the plots; nothing on the page needs to change.
